newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Air France to face legal flak over 1994 rescue plan.
newsitem.headline: Air France to face legal flak over 1994 rescue plan.

text.p: Air France and the European Commission are set next week to face legal scrutiny of the airline's 20-billion-franc ($3.4 billion) rescue plan when the EU court holds an oral hearing into the 1994 aid package.

The state-owned airline won Commission approval for the bale-out plan in 1994, a decision since challenged by a posse of companies led by British Airways, SAS and Dutch airline KLM, among others, and supported by the British, Danish, Swedish and Norwegian governments.

The European Court of First Instance, which will hear the case on Tuesday and possibly Wednesday, must weigh points made at the hearing before rejecting the challengers' arguments or annulling the original Commission decision to clear the aid.
Next week is only a hearing, with no initial decision due before July and no final ruling likely before the year end.

Central to the case are questions about whether the Commission, under EU state aid rules, was justified in approving the full 20 billion francs sought by Air France and whether it erred in choosing a time-limit for its approval conditions.

Other questions relate to Air France's relationship with its former domestic subsidiary Air Inter, now Air France Europe, with parties set to argue over whether the Commission took sufficient account of their likely merger.

Also at issue is whether the Commission should have applied to Air Inter the conditions imposed to prevent Air France from incurring debt, buying stakes in other airlines, increasing capacity or using the cash to cut fares.
State aid and its use or abuse has long dominated the civil aviation debate in Europe, with private carriers complaining about what they see as the blank cheques written out for state-owned airlines.
The Commission counters the charge by saying it is duty bound to neutrality on public-versus-private ownership and adds that state-owned firms must be able to raise fresh capital.
Recent years have seen the Commission approve aid to Air France, Spain's Iberia, TAP Air Portugal, Greece's Olympic Airways and Ireland's Aer Lingus.
Alitalia 's restructuring plan, accompanied by a clearance request for more than three trillion lire ($1.7 billion), is on the Commission's table now.
Next week's case is seen by the challengers as pivotal in the debate about what level of state aid is fair.
"It's a landmark case, that's absolutely clear," said one source from the challengers' camp.
"If it goes their way then it would be a significant setback both for the airline industry but presumably also for other industries affected by state aid.

"It would be an admission that this kind of behaviour is allowed and where then is the limit? If you look at the decision taken by the Commission it's full of holes, it's easy to circumvent and it's unclear," the source added.
One competition lawyer close to the case was not so impressed by the prospect of either possible outcome, saying the court's rulings had often proved inconclusive in the past.
Even the worst case scenario for the Commission, that the court annulled its decision on the grounds of "manifest error" in law, would likely be no more than embarrassing.
Were the Commission to pass up the opportunity to appeal, reaching a new decision would still take another year with the analysis and hearings, taking the parties to the end of 1998.
Air France could appeal any subsequent decision to cut back the aid, starting off the legal merry-go-round once again until some time around 2001.

"Who knows where Air France will be then? The money would have been spent on Air France's restructuring plan between 1994 and 1996. Would the Commission seriously ask the French government to pay back the money then?" he asked.
